# Transit of the Nine Planets

The Dwadasa Bhava Phala Chandrika explains the movement and retrograde motion of the nine planets in relation to the Sun. Mercury and Venus, being swift planets with greater speed than Earth, do not require the Sun to overtake them. Instead, these planets themselves move ahead of the Sun and subsequently experience retrograde motion. Mercury can advance up to 28 degrees ahead of the Sun before slowing and moving backward, maintaining a distance of approximately 22 degrees during retrograde phases. Depending on the zodiacal sign, Mercury may occasionally retrograde as much as 14 degrees ahead of the Sun.

The retrograde motion of planets is not actual backward movement but rather appears so from Earth's perspective due to relative distances and orbital positions. The maximum retrograde extents vary by planet: Mercury reaches approximately 16 degrees and 30 minutes; Venus similarly about 16 degrees and 30 minutes; Mars about 10 to 9 degrees; Jupiter about 10 degrees; and Saturn about 6 degrees and 58 minutes. The outer planets Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto also exhibit retrograde motion, though the classical Vedic tradition does not employ these in calculations, as the ancient sages determined their influence upon human life to be negligible.

The text further describes planetary states and their strengths, as well as various systems of measuring years used in classical Indian astronomy, including lunar, solar, savana, Jupiterian, and sidereal year systems.

# On Retrogradation and Planetary Weakness

The text presented does not directly address retrogradation itself. Instead, it discusses *astaṅgatva* — the condition of planetary invisibility or weakness that arises when planets pass behind the Sun or become obscured from Earth's view.

Five planets orbit the Sun (the Moon excepted). Mercury and Venus, whose orbits lie within Earth's orbit, move faster than Earth and periodically pass behind the Sun (*prāk astaṅgatva* and *paścād astaṅgatva*), becoming invisible. Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, whose orbits lie beyond Earth's orbit, move more slowly than Earth. As Earth completes its orbit and moves ahead of these outer planets, they appear to recede toward the opposite side of the Sun, entering a state called *astaṅgatva*.

When planets are in *astaṅgatva*, they are considerably weakened. The text illustrates this through precise distances: Mercury becomes 2.26 times weaker when invisible compared to when direct; Venus becomes 6.23 times weaker; Mars becomes 4.8 times weaker; Jupiter becomes 1.22 times weaker; and Saturn becomes 1.1 times weaker.

Because Jupiter governs auspicious religious rites, wealth, and progeny, and Venus governs marriage and marital happiness, auspicious ceremonies are avoided during their periods of invisibility. Similarly, the Moon's invisibility on new moon days prevents such ceremonies. This weakening is attributed to the Sun blocking the planets' rays from reaching Earth, diminishing their beneficial influence on human affairs.

# Panchanga: The Five Limbs of Time

The classical Vedic astronomical tradition recognizes five principal divisions of time, known together as the Panchanga, or five limbs. These divisions structure the measurement and interpretation of celestial movements and their effects upon earthly matters.

The text presented discusses the foundational principles governing how planets move through the sky and how their positions impart varying degrees of strength and influence. Mercury and Venus, being inferior planets that orbit between the Earth and Sun, experience two distinct conjunctions with the Sun—one superior and one inferior—which determines their visibility and rising or setting positions. Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, being superior planets beyond Earth's orbit, follow different patterns of visibility, setting in the west and rising in the east.

The text further elaborates on the Shadbala, or six sources of planetary strength. These are sthanabala (positional strength), digbala (directional strength), chestabala (motional strength), kalabala (temporal strength), drigbala (aspectual strength), and naisargika bala (natural inherent strength). Each of these dimensions determines how effectively a planet yields its results at any given moment.

The planets derive additional power or weakness based on their placement in the zodiac, their position relative to the angles of a natal chart, the time of day or night, the lunar phase, and their aspects from other planets. Through understanding these five dimensions of time and the six sources of strength, the astrologer discerns the true efficacy of planetary influences.

# Combustion (Astangata) in Classical Vedic Astrology

The concept of combustion, or astangata, describes the condition when a planet comes into proximity with the Sun and thereby loses its independent strength and beneficial effects. According to the Dwadasa Bhava Phala Chandrika, when a planet is situated too close to the Sun, its significations become diminished or obscured, much as a lamp's light fades when placed near the bright radiance of the Sun itself.

The text explains that planetary influence operates through both the planet itself and its associated houses or fields. When auspicious planets aspect a planet or its fields, all of that planet's significations are enhanced and become thoroughly beneficial. However, when a planet falls under combustion due to proximity to the Sun, these natural strengths are compromised.

The severity of combustion's effects varies based on the degree of affliction. If only the planet itself comes under malefic influence, approximately thirty-three percent of its beneficence remains. When both the planet and one of its associated fields receive malefic planetary aspects, this reduces to sixty-six percent of beneficial effects. Complete combustion—when both the planet and its fields are afflicted—may reduce the planet's beneficial nature substantially.

The text illustrates this through examples: a well-placed Venus in the fifth house may demonstrate creative talent and imaginative power, yet if Venus and its associated fields lack auspicious planetary support, the artistic expression becomes incomplete or lacks full refinement.

# Planetary Position, Conjunction, and Aspect

The text presents foundational concepts in Vedic astrology concerning how planets influence the zodiacal signs. Planetary position refers to identifying which signs contain which planets within the zodiacal wheel. When planets occupy the same location, their conjunction creates a condition wherein the planets influence one another. Planetary aspect describes how planets direct their influence upon particular signs even when not physically present in them.

The ancient sages transmitted to us the knowledge governing planetary position, conjunction, and aspect. This wisdom is applied here with reasoned methodology. The text explains that each zodiacal sign measures thirty degrees. When a planet occupies the beginning of a sign, its influence extends throughout that entire thirty-degree span.

However, a distinction emerges regarding planets situated near the end of a sign. According to the teachings of the sages, planets at the end of a sign occupy a weakened state and possess diminished strength. Though weakened, their influence still extends across the standard thirty-degree measure. Therefore, the influence of such planets reaches backward from their position to thirty degrees before it.

The text illustrates this principle through specific examples: Mercury in Pisces, Jupiter in Aries, and Mars in Leo. These examples demonstrate how planetary influence operates according to the degree position within each sign, with the planet's strength determining the quality of that influence upon the signs it touches.

# Shadbalamulu: Six-fold Strength in Classical Vedic Astrology

The concept of planetary strength, as explained in classical texts, rests upon understanding how planets influence one another across the zodiac through their rays and degrees of separation. Each planet possesses an orb of influence extending thirty degrees forward from its own position, and similarly exerts influence upon planets positioned thirty degrees behind it.

The foundational principle is that planets situated behind another planet may conjoin and influence it, whereas planets positioned ahead cannot affect those behind them. This directionality is essential to determining conjugal relationships and mutual strength between celestial bodies.

When two planets occupy different signs, their actual degrees of separation must be measured precisely, as no celestial boundaries divide the zodiacal circle. A planet's rays extend through the intermediate space until they reach the second planet. The remaining distance—calculated by subtracting the separation from thirty degrees—indicates the strength of influence one planet exerts upon another.

Through specific examples involving the Sun, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the Moon, the text demonstrates how to measure these intervals and assess consequent strength. Even planets in the same sign may exercise minimal influence if their degree separation is considerable. # The Concept of Planetary Significations and Bhava Trayam

The text from the Dwadasa Bhava Phala Chandrika presents foundational principles governing how planetary aspects affect natal interpretation. The discourse establishes methods for calculating the strength of planetary aspects by measuring angular distances and subtracting these from a standard thirty-degree span to determine the degree of influence exerted upon aspected planets or houses.

The text then addresses a classical problem that has occupied Vedic scholars since ancient times: when a single planet rules two different houses, which house's results should be attributed to that planet's influence? This ambiguity has created considerable scholarly debate. The text resolves this through the system called Bhava Trayam, or the "triple house method."

Rather than assigning a planet solely to one house's rulership, the system considers three factors together: the house itself, its ruling planet, and the ruling planet's own house of rulership. These three elements are analyzed collectively to determine the complete results attributed to any given house. For example, the Lagna Trayam encompasses the first house, its lord, and that lord's own house of residence. Similarly, each of the twelve houses receives examination through this triple framework.

This methodology acknowledges that when a planet governs multiple houses, its beneficial or challenging effects flow through both houses simultaneously. By evaluating all three components together rather than in isolation, astrologers arrive at more comprehensive and accurate interpretations of a chart's indications, thereby addressing the longstanding ambiguity in planetary house rulership assessment.

# Graha Drishti: Planetary Aspects in the Tula Lagna

Graha Drishti refers to the directional influences that planets cast upon the natal houses and their governing lords. This classical concept examines how planetary aspects distribute their effects across the trinities of houses—particularly the first house trinity (lagna, its lord, and the second house of the lagna's lord).

In the illustrated example of Tula lagna, Rahu positioned at twenty-four degrees in Mesha casts its aspect across specific degrees. The text demonstrates that Rahu's influence extends from Mesha's twenty-fourth degree through Vrishabha's twenty-fourth degree, affecting the lagna trinity with a combined strength of thirty degrees. Similarly, Ketu's aspect touches portions of both the lagna and the lagna lord's second house, totaling thirty degrees of influence.

Mars restricts its effect to merely the lagna lord's second house, while the Moon's aspect spans from Mesha's twenty-ninth degree through Vrishabha's twenty-ninth degree, creating a combined impact of thirty-six degrees on the lagna trinity. Jupiter's seventh and ninth aspects extend their reach across multiple houses, with calculations determining precise degree measurements of influence.

The text emphasizes that these aspectual strengths vary by planet and must be precisely calculated by degree. # The Principles of Position, Conjunction, and Aspect in Classical Vedic Astrology

The classical framework of planetary influence operates through three fundamental mechanisms: *sthithi* (position), *yuti* (conjunction), and *veekshana* (aspect).

**Position** refers to a planet's stationary effect within a particular zodiacal sign or house. A planet exerts influence across the degrees it occupies, extending from its exact position backward through the sign's concluding degrees.

**Conjunction** occurs when a planet directly contacts another planet or house lord through proximity. The strength of this connection is measured in degrees, calculated as the interval between the aspecting planet and the contacted entity. This distance is then converted within a thirty-degree scale to determine the precise influence conveyed.

**Aspect** represents a planet's directional viewing power toward specific zodiacal regions. Different planets possess different aspect capacities—for instance, certain planets cast seventh aspects while others cast fourth, eighth, or ninth aspects. The aspect's influence begins from the aspecting planet's exact degree and extends backward through the relevant zodiacal zones.

In practical application, these three mechanisms are combined to assess a planet's total effect upon a house trinity. The degrees contributed through position, conjunction, and aspect are summed together, yielding the comprehensive influence a planet exercises over the threefold divisions of a particular house. Whether a planet's overall influence proves auspicious or unfavorable depends upon its natural benefic or malefic character relative to the natal chart's ascendant.

# The Triadic House Method in Vedic Astrology

The Triadic House Method, as presented in the Dwadasa Bhava Phala Chandrika, is a systematic approach to evaluating planetary influences across the twelve houses of a birth chart by grouping them into four sets of three houses each.

Under this method, each house is considered alongside its corresponding triad group. When analyzing a planet's aspect or influence, the text measures the degrees of impact on each house within that triad. The strength of influence is determined quantitatively: aspects measuring less than fifteen minutes of arc are considered negligible and omitted from consideration; influences reaching thirty degrees are understood as moderately potent; and those exceeding thirty degrees indicate increased strength.

The method distinguishes between benefic and malefic planetary effects on each triadic group. Benefic planets (those functioning favorably for the ascendant) are understood to strengthen their respective houses, while malefic planets correspondingly weaken them. The text provides detailed tables presenting these influences across all four triads, allowing one to readily comprehend which planets benefit or burden particular houses and to what degree.

A remarkable principle emerges: the planetary influences affecting the ninth house triad (fortune and destiny) are considered identical to those affecting the twelfth house triad (loss and expenses). This creates a balanced correspondence in the framework.

The practical application relies on observing planetary periods. When benefic planetary influences manifest during favorable periods, auspicious outcomes are predicted; conversely, malefic planetary periods produce unfavorable results.

# Benefic and Malefic Planet Determination for the Twelve Signs

The text presented is primarily a technical exposition on calculating sunrise times and ascendant determinations for natal chart purposes, rather than a direct treatment of benefic and malefic planet classification across the twelve signs.

The passage demonstrates the methodology for establishing accurate birth time calculations using latitude and longitude adjustments. For any given date, sunrise times are established at a baseline latitude, then adjusted proportionally based on the observer's actual latitude. Similarly, longitudinal differences are applied, with corrections increasing or decreasing the local time depending on whether one is positioned east or west of the reference meridian of 82.5 degrees.

The text illustrates these principles through a worked example: a birth occurring on April 21, 2004 at 11:30 PM at 15 degrees north latitude and 77.5 degrees east longitude. The sunrise time for that date and latitude is calculated as 6:02 AM (Indian Standard Time). From this foundation, the ascendant sign at birth is determined by calculating the precise degree and minute of the zodiac rising at the moment of birth.

The passage emphasizes that astrologers should independently calculate sunrise times and ascendant measurements according to their own geographic coordinates, rather than relying solely on external almanac sources. This ensures accuracy in determining the natal ascendant, which forms the foundation for all subsequent astrological analysis and interpretation.

# The Second Lord and Its Effects on Physical Well-being

The Dwadasa Bhava Phala Chandrika describes how the lord of the second house influences the native's physical comfort and family circumstances through its position, aspect, and conjunction with other planets.

When the second lord is malefic and afflicts the first three houses, the native experiences diminished comfort arising from various sources. Family discord, opposition from people in society, and reduced nourishment cause the face to appear sorrowful. The native may seem distressed, either through diminished eating comfort or through lack of cooperation from family members. Speech becomes harsh, and family discord leads to weakened bodily strength.

Conversely, when the second lord is benefic and favorably influences the first three houses, the native enjoys comfort, prosperity, and gentle speech. Family members offer cooperation and support, allowing the native to appear physically vigorous, cheerful, and contented. Physical comfort increases, and those in one's environment—both family and community—become sources of assistance.

The specific planetary lord of the second house carries particular significance. When the Sun holds this position as benefic, paternal support enhances bodily comfort; when malefic, it increases bodily strain through the father. The Moon as a benefic second lord brings abundant nourishment and maternal comfort, while as a malefic it causes deficiency in nourishment and bathing facilities. Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn each govern different family relationships and determine whether comfort or strain results through parents, siblings, relatives, and servants. These effects flow naturally from each planet's characteristic influence over the second house.

# The Golden Rules of Chart Reading

The assessment of planetary strength forms the foundation of accurate chart interpretation. According to the Dwadasa Bhava Phala Chandrika, six qualities establish whether a planet proves beneficial or weakened in its effects.

A planet demonstrates strength when it occupies its own sign, receives favorable transit influence, remains in its own period and sub-period, moves retrograde, stands behind other planets in zodiacal position, and governs a larger degree span over a bhava. Conversely, weakness arises when a planet occupies an enemy's sign, lacks transit support, passes through its own period's sub-period already completed, remains stationary or combusted, stands ahead in position, and governs fewer degrees.

The proximity of beneficial planets to harmful ones requires careful consideration. When a beneficial planet influences a bhava across a greater degree span than a harmful planet, the beneficial result predominates—particularly if the harmful planet lacks transit strength. Should the beneficial planet complete its own period's sub-period, its strength reduces by half, yet its results still manifest if transit supports it. Conversely, strong planetary combinations prove ineffective without favorable transit influence.

The text emphasizes that transit strength (gochara) stands paramount in determining manifestation of results. A single planet may inherit up to six strengths or weaknesses. The astrologer must examine each combination carefully, as even weakened planets yield full results when transit conditions prove favorable, while apparently strong planets produce no effects without such support.
